csr.question: According to the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2023 report, what were the major reasons driving food insecurity in 2023?

answer.summary: According to SOFI 2023, the major drivers of food insecurity and malnutrition were the intensification and interaction of conflict, climate extremes, economic slowdowns and downturns, and growing inequality. The report also highlights high prices for food, agricultural inputs and energy—linked to the war in Ukraine and post-pandemic economic effects—as key pressures keeping hunger above pre-COVID-19 levels. Urbanization is treated as a major megatrend reshaping agrifood systems and access to affordable healthy diets, rather than a standalone shock driver.

findings.claim: SOFI 2023 identifies conflict, climate extremes, economic slowdowns and downturns, and growing inequality as the major drivers of food insecurity and malnutrition, often occurring in combination.

The COVID-19 pandemic, the subsequent economic rebound, the war in Ukraine, and soaring prices of food, agricultural inputs and energy affected regions differently and contributed to hunger remaining far above pre-pandemic levels.
Highly unaffordable nutritious foods, combined with conflict, climate extremes, economic slowdowns/downturns and inequalities, pushed the world off track for SDG 2.

Regional impacts differed: for example, Southern Africa’s hunger increase was linked to inflation from international commodity prices, domestic unemployment, and vulnerability to shocks; Western Asia faced political instability, conflict, supply disruptions, inflation, and food shortages.
Urbanization was highlighted in SOFI 2023 as a megatrend transforming agrifood systems and affecting access to affordable healthy diets across the rural–urban continuum.

risks_assumptions: The answer reflects the SOFI 2023 report’s framing; where the report discusses 2022 hunger outcomes, those are used as the latest assessment context available in the 2023 publication.

confidence.reason: The drivers are directly stated in multiple SOFI 2023 passages, with supporting examples of regional variation and price/inflation effects.

sources.title: FAO SOFI 2023: The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World
sources.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY This year, the update to the global assessment of food security and nutrition reflects a particular moment in history. While the pandemic, the ensuing economic rebound, the war in Ukraine, and soaring prices of food, agricultural inputs and energy have all played out differently across regions with differing impacts, new estimates indicate hunger is no longer on the rise at the global level but is still far above pre-COVID-19-pandemic levels and far off track to achieve Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 2. As past editions of this report have highlighted, the intensification of the major drivers of food insecurity and malnutrition – conflict, climate extremes, economic slowdowns and downturns, and growing inequality – often occurring in combination, is challenging our efforts to achieve the SDGs. There is no question these threats will continue, requiring that we remain steadfast to build resilience against them. However, there are still important megatrends that must be fully understood when devising policies to meet the SDG 2 targets. One such megatrend, and the focus of this year’s report, is urbanization. As urbanization increases, rural and urban areas are becoming more intertwined, and the spatial distinction between them is becoming more fluid.

As a result, hunger remains far above pre-pandemic levels globally and in all regions. At the regional level, this dynamic of income and price effect is visible in multiple subregions, with varying results. In Southern Africa , for instance, the uptick of hunger in 2022 stemmed from increasing inflation, following the upsurge in international commodity prices, as well as domestic challenges such as persistently high levels of unemployment and vulnerability to shocks. 11 Although there was sustained GDP growth in 2022, this often did not translate into improved socioeconomic conditions for the poor. Agricultural production, at the same time, suffered from severe droughts and floods, and the surge in international fertilizer prices. In Middle Africa, the increase in hunger has mainly resulted from food inflation and increasing food import bills, as well as extreme climate events, which have counteracted the positive effects of economic growth, driven by buoyant oil export revenues in some countries.

sources.text: FOREWORD We have repeatedly highlighted that the intensification and interaction of conflict, climate extremes and economic slowdowns and downturns, combined with highly unaffordable nutritious foods and growing inequalities, are pushing us off track to meet the SDG 2 targets. While we must remain steadfast in taking bold targeted actions to build resilience against these adversities, other important megatrends must be considered. Urbanization, for example, is one such megatrend that features as the theme of this year’s report. By 2050, almost seven in ten people are projected to live in cities; but even today, this proportion is approximately 56 percent. Urbanization is shaping agrifood systems in ways we can only understand through a rural–urban continuum lens, encompassing everything from food production, food processing, and food distribution, marketing and procurement, to consumer behaviour. Due to population growth, small and intermediate cities and rural towns are increasingly bridging the space between rural areas and large metropolises. Hence, in our efforts to end hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition in an urbanizing world, we can no longer operate on the traditional assumption of a rural–urban divide. As the world is urbanizing, food demand and supply are changing rapidly across the rural–urban continuum, challenging our traditional thinking.
